power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: As healthcare systems increasingly emphasize value-based care, evidence regarding the economic implications of nonpharmacologic interventions is needed to inform implementation and reimbursement decisions.

This study aimed to assess the economic value of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction, identify clinical populations in which economic evaluations have been conducted, and assess the strength of the available economic evidence.
All clinical populations and healthcare settings.
This systematic review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Metaanalyses 2020 guidelines and was prospectively registered (CRD420250648516).
Nine databases, including MEDLINE, Embase and Scopus, were searched from inception through March 2026 without language restriction, with reference-list screening and citation tracking.
Eligible studies evaluated Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction and at least one economic outcome.

Two reviewers independently screened records, extracted data, and assessed quality using the Quality of Health Economic Studies instrument and the Consolidated Health Economic Evaluation Reporting Standards 2022 checklist.
Among 468 identified records, 12 economic evaluations met inclusion criteria.
Studies included 8 randomized clinical trials, 2 Markov models, and 2 prospective cohort studies, conducted in North America (6) and Europe (6).
Chronic pain conditions were most frequent (6), followed by mental health disorders (3), breast cancer survivorship (2), and pulmonary arterial hypertension (1).

Across these populations, reductions in healthcare utilization and productivity losses generally offset delivery costs, resulting in lower overall costs with equivalent or improved health outcomes for Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction compared with treatment-as-usual.
Results were also favorable or comparable relative to active comparators including cognitive behavioral therapy.

Despite intervention costs of $195 to $866 per participant (mean, $461), all cost-utility analyses comparing Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction with treatment-as-usual over at least 6 months reported lower costs with equivalent or improved outcomes.
Methodological quality was high, with 10 of 12 studies meeting above 80% quality criteria and 5 achieving 100% adherence.
Reporting transparency was generally strong.
Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction was associated with favorable economic outcomes across chronic pain, mental health, and breast cancer survivorship populations.

Current evidence suggests that MBSR may represent a high-value nonpharmacologic intervention, with reductions in healthcare utilization and productivity losses frequently offsetting intervention costs.
Additional economic evaluations are needed in underrepresented populations, healthcare settings, and delivery models.
 This is the first systematic review focused exclusively on the economic value of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) independent of other mindfulness-based interventions.
 A comprehensive search strategy was developed with librarian support, peer reviewed using the PRESS checklist, and applied across nine databases without language restrictions.

 Economic evidence was evaluated using established frameworks for both methodological quality (QHES) and reporting transparency (CHEERS 2022), with assessments conducted independently by multiple reviewers.

 Included studies represented diverse clinical populations, healthcare settings, economic perspectives, and evaluation types, allowing assessment of economic outcomes across a broad range of contexts.

 Substantial heterogeneity in populations, comparators, cost inputs, perspectives, and time horizons precluded quantitative pooling of results, and available evidence was largely limited to North America and Europe.

Healthcare systems worldwide face growing challenges from chronic pain, mental health disorders, stressrelated illness, and cancer survivorship, conditions associated with high healthcare utilization, disability, and escalating costs. 1 2 Chronic pain affects approximately 25% of US adults with annual costs of $722.8 billion, 3 while major depressive disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder carry estimated annual economic burdens of $382.4 billion and $232.2 billion, respectively. 4 5 Anxiety and other stress-related conditions are similarly linked to lost productivity and diminished quality of life. 6 7 These challenges, alongside provider shortages and concerns regarding opioid use and long-term pharmacologic management, have increased interest in effective, scalable nonpharmacologic care approaches. [8] [9] [10] [11] Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR), developed by Jon Kabat-Zinn in 1979, is among the most widely disseminated and standardized mindfulness-based interventions. 12 Delivered primarily in groups, MBSR integrates meditation, gentle yoga, and psychoeducation to cultivate awareness and adaptive responses to physical and emotional distress. 13  14 Randomized clinical trials (RCTs) and metaanalyses demonstrate benefits for psychological distress, health-related quality of life, pain-related outcomes, and stress symptoms across diverse populations. [15] [16] [17] [18] [19] [20] Despite this evidence base, MBSR integration into healthcare delivery and reimbursement systems remains limited outside programs such as the Veterans Health Administration Whole Health System. [21] [22] [23] Broader implementation requires evidence of both clinical benefit and economic value. 24 25 Previous systematic reviews suggest mindfulness-based interventions may be cost-effective; however, most combined MBSR with other third-wave interventions, including Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy and Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, limiting MBSR-specific conclusions. [26] [27] [28] Furthermore, MBSR economic evaluations have been published since the latest comprehensive reviews. 29 30 Therefore, an updated synthesis focused specifically on MBSR is warranted.

text.text: The recommendations in this systematic review were informed by integrated knowledge translation research (IKT) involving health insurers, policymakers, healthcare administrators, clinicians, MBSR teacher-trainers and teachers, and patients. 31 These groups identified cost-effectiveness of MBSR as needed to understand in order to advance access to MBSR. 31 The objective of this systematic review was to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of MBSR across clinical populations and healthcare settings, and the quality of the available economic evidence.

text.text: No restrictions were placed on population, setting, study design, follow-up duration, comparator, or moderator.
Results were classified by type of economic evaluation and health condition.
The research librarian (LH), along with experts in mindfulness and health economics, developed an Ovid MEDLINE search using MeSH terms and keywords for MBSR and economic evaluation.

A second librarian peer-reviewed it using the PRESS (Peer Review of Electronic Search Strategies) checklist. 37 The final search was run in Ovid MEDLINE and translated for Embase, Scopus, APA PsycINFO, the NHS Economic Evaluation Database (NHS EED), the International HTA Database, ProQuest Dissertations and Theses, the Tufts Cost-Effectiveness Analysis Registry, and CINAHL.

text.text: Two reviewers (RLA, RG) independently extracted study characteristics, intervention and comparator details, economic perspectives, costing methods, time horizons, uncertainty analyses, and reported economic outcomes.
Because this review sought to synthesize all forms of economic evaluation, no single primary type of economic evaluation was prespecified.

Included studies reported a broad range of economic components and evaluation types, including intervention delivery costs, healthcare utilization costs, direct and indirect costs, implementation costs, cost-effectiveness outcomes, and cost-utility outcomes.

Cost-utility analyses (CUAs) reporting incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) in terms of cost per increase in qualityadjusted life-years (QALYs) were considered the most rigorous and policy-relevant analyses, thus were prioritized in the synthesis when available.
Economic findings were synthesized narratively across clinical populations, analytic perspectives, comparator types, and economic evaluation types.

Meta-analysis of economic outcomes was not performed because economic evaluations often differ in the cost components included and other context-and setting-specific factors, including healthcare delivery, resource use, implementation, and local cost structures, limiting the transferability and interpretability of pooled economic estimates. [39] [40] [41] Accordingly, interpretation focused on the overall direction and consistency of economic findings rather than pooled quantitative estimates.

text.text: Comparator interventions were categorized as treatment-as-usual (TAU) when MBSR was compared to any form of usual standard care.
Economic perspectives were classified according to cost inputs rather than author-reported terminology and grouped into 3 categories: payer, healthcare sector, and societal.

The payer perspective included direct healthcare costs reimbursed by a healthcare payer; the healthcare sector perspective included all direct healthcare costs regardless of who pays; and the societal perspective included both healthcare and non-healthcare costs, including productivity losses, no matter who pays. 42 43 To facilitate interpretation of economic findings across studies, CUA results were mapped onto a cost-effectiveness decision matrix categorizing interventions according to relative differences in costs and health outcomes (e.g., lower cost with improved outcomes).

text.text: The literature search identified 468 records across databases, with one additional study identified through citation searching (eFigure 1 -PRISMA Flow Diagram).
After removal of duplicates, 287 records underwent title and abstract screening, and 67 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility.
In total, 12 economic evaluations met the inclusion criteria (eTable 4).
Study characteristics, cost inputs and analytic perspectives, and economic outcomes are summarized in Tables 1, 2, and 3, respectively.
Five economic evaluations were conducted in the United States, six from four European countries (Spain, Denmark, Sweden, and the United Kingdom), and one in Canada.
Eight were full economic evaluations using CUA, including six primary trial-based evaluations and two simulation modeling studies.

Three studies were partial economic evaluations, and one was a pilot feasibility study assessing intervention delivery costs and the feasibility of collecting healthcare utilization data for a future economic evaluation.

Study design included 8 RCTs, 2 prospective cohort trials, and 2 mathematical modeling studies using decision-analytic (Markov) models that synthesized evidence from multiple sources and simulated transitions between health states to estimate costs and health outcomes.
Chronic pain-related conditions were the most studied population (6), followed by mental health disorders (3), breast cancer survivorship (2), and pulmonary arterial hypertension (1).
Cost inputs varied across studies.
Using the QHES instrument to evaluate methodological quality of the included economic evaluations (eTable 2), 33 five studies achieved a perfect QHES score, meeting 100% of assessed criteria.

text.text: Common methodological limitations included limited discussion of the direction and magnitude of potential biases (6 studies), incomplete handling of uncertainty through sensitivity analyses (5 studies), and time horizons that were deemed insufficient to capture all relevant outcomes (3 studies).

Partial economic evaluations were additionally limited by the absence of QALY-based outcomes and reduced ability to provide a formal assessment of cost-effectiveness relative to alternative interventions.
Across the 12 studies, reporting was strong for the descriptive CHEERS items (eTable 3), and all but one study disclosed funding sources.
Notable methodological gaps were observed.
Only 2 studies reported a formal health economic analysis plan, use of discount rates, or patient/stakeholder engagement.
Only 1 study described how patient/stakeholder engagement influenced findings, and only 1 considered equity.
Four studies did not include the currency/price year.
Economic findings were generally favorable across health conditions (Table 3 and Figure 1; details in eAppendix 3).

text.text: Overall, the most consistent results were observed in chronic pain-related conditions, where multiple trial-based and model-based economic evaluations (k=6) demonstrated dominance of MBSR over TAU (health improvements and cost savings) from the payer, healthcare, and societal perspectives in a variety of settings.

The two modeling studies predicted greater economic value for older adults (aged ≥80 years) 47 and those with more severe pain. 47 48 Studies in mental health conditions (k=3) similarly reported lower costs with comparable or improved health outcomes relative to usual care from all perspectives, and in several settings.

text.text: Evidence among breast cancer survivors was more limited (k=2) but included one recent CUA demonstrating lower costs and improved outcomes from the payer and societal perspectives compared with an active control intervention.
A single feasibility-focused study in pulmonary arterial hypertension evaluated implementation costs but did not assess comparative cost-effectiveness.

text.text: TAU reflected heterogeneous standard care approaches varying by population and level of care.
Relative to evidence-based behavioral therapies, MBSR demonstrated economically favorable or comparable outcomes.

Compared with a frontline behavioral treatment, specifically CBT, MBSR was associated with lower costs and comparable health outcomes for those with chronic low back pain. 49 Similarly, compared with attachment-based compassion therapy (ABCT), MBSR produced marginally greater health benefits at slightly higher cost for mental health patients. 29 MBSR also performed favorably when compared with other active comparators, including educational, attention-matched, and self-management interventions designed to control nonspecific treatment effects.

text.text: Studies that evaluated more than one perspective reported similar findings across perspectives.
Use of the payer perspective was most prevalent (9 studies).
A healthcare sector perspective was used in two studies, and a societal perspective was used in seven; several studies reported more than one perspective.

From the healthcare and payer perspectives, across studies conducted in various health systems in North America and Europe, the cost savings associated with MBSR were driven by reduced healthcare utilization.
Common contributors included decreases in outpatient visits, primary care encounters, hospital admissions, emergency department utilization, diagnostic testing, and laboratory costs.

Specifically, studies reported fewer emergency room visits, hospitalizations, and diagnostic tests among individuals with breast cancer, 30 fewer primary care visits among individuals with mental health conditions, 29 and reductions in both condition-related and unrelated costs among individuals with chronic low back pain. 49 From the societal perspective, cost savings reflected both reduced healthcare use and improvements in workplace functioning, including reduced absenteeism and productivity losses among individuals with fibromyalgia, 50 and reductions in disability pension use in pain populations. 51

text.text: Uncertainty and sensitivity analyses were conducted in seven studies using methods such as nonparametric bootstrapping, probabilistic sensitivity analyses, scenario analyses, and cost-effectiveness acceptability curves.

Overall, these analyses generally supported the robustness of the primary findings, with economic conclusions remaining favorable across a range of assumptions despite uncertainty in some incremental cost estimates.
Detailed descriptions and results of the uncertainty and sensitivity analyses are provided in eAppendix 4.
Time horizons ranged from 8 weeks to 5 years, with one study projecting 20 years. 52 Most findings used a 1-year time horizon.

text.text: To our knowledge, this systematic review is the first to focus exclusively on the economic value of MBSR independent of other mindfulness-based interventions.

Although economic evaluations are inherently context-dependent, studies conducted across diverse healthcare settings and analytic perspectives reached similar conclusions regarding the economic value of MBSR.

Across chronic pain, mental health, and breast cancer survivorship populations, MBSR was associated with favorable economic outcomes, with reductions in healthcare utilization and productivity losses generally offsetting intervention costs and often resulting in overall cost savings (Figure 1).

text.text: Findings were consistent across heterogeneous settings and study designs, including randomized clinical trials, prospective cohort studies, and decision-analytic models.
Methodological quality was generally rated high, with 10 of 12 studies meeting more than 80% of QHES criteria, and reporting transparency generally strong according to CHEERS 2022.
The largest number of studies were observed in chronic pain-related populations, which accounted for half of the 12 included studies.
Across low back pain, fibromyalgia, and mixed chronic pain-related conditions, MBSR consistently demonstrated cost savings, favorable cost-effectiveness, or both.
Given the burden of chronic pain, these findings suggest it may be among the strongest candidates for broader implementation and reimbursement of MBSR.

Modeling simulations further suggest that economic benefits may be even greater among older adults and those with more severe pain, highlighting the importance of future research aimed at identifying the patient subgroups most likely to derive clinical and economic benefit.
As expected, results were more favorable when MBSR was compared to TAU rather than active controls.

Importantly, however, MBSR remained economically competitive with established psychotherapies, producing outcomes similar to CBT at lower cost and comparable economic value compared with other active behavioral interventions.

Because MBSR was cost-effective at conventional thresholds and compared favorably with CBT, a therapy already reimbursed and guideline-recommended for chronic pain, these findings support consideration of MBSR as a reimbursable option in routine care. 54 Although MBSR requires an upfront investment (mean intervention cost, approximately $461 per participant), these costs were frequently offset by fewer primary care visits, emergency department visits, hospitalizations, and diagnostic tests.

text.text: Most evaluations examined costs and outcomes no longer than 6 or 12 months.
Although this timeframe captures many relevant costs and outcomes, it may not fully reflect longer-term economic consequences.
The favorable findings observed within these follow-up periods suggest that MBSR can generate economic value in the near to medium term.

Future research should evaluate whether these benefits are sustained over longer periods and whether strategies such as booster sessions or digital supports are needed to maintain long-term clinical and economic gains.
Despite favorable economic evidence, integration of MBSR into routine care remains limited.
This gap may reflect reimbursement barriers, implementation challenges, workforce constraints, and limited awareness of the growing economic evidence base.

Notably, mindfulness-based interventions are recommended within contemporary nonpharmacologic approaches to chronic pain management, yet coverage and adoption remain inconsistent across healthcare settings. 55  56 A 2026 multisite RCT (n=451) demonstrated that MBSR delivered through health insurance-reimbursable group medical visits resulted in significant reductions in pain intensity and pain interference, with benefits maintained for up to one year. 57 In that trial, MBSR was delivered in 2-hour sessions (consistent with the original MBSR format), to groups of 4 to 14 participants, without a retreat day, to align with existing insurance reimbursement structures. 58 In 2026, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, stated that group medical visits typically occur within 60-to 120-minute time blocks and further proposed limiting reimbursement to a maximum session duration of 60 minutes. 59 Because current evidence for mindfulness-based programs is derived primarily from 120-to 150-minute sessions, the effectiveness of shorter reimbursable formats remains uncertain.

text.text: Reimbursement policies should therefore consider aligning covered session durations with the formats evaluated in clinical and economic studies.
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings.
Included studies demonstrated substantial heterogeneity in economic perspectives, cost inputs, healthcare settings, currencies, time horizons, comparators, and patient populations.
Despite this variability, findings were consistent across studies.
Evaluations were conducted exclusively in North America and Europe.

Most focused on chronic pain, mental health conditions, or breast cancer survivorship, and used follow-up periods of approximately 1 year or less, limiting generalizability to other regions, settings, health conditions, and longer-term economic effects.
In addition, none of the identified studies evaluated online or hybrid MBSR delivery models, representing an important evidence gap given increasing interest in scalable implementation approaches.

Economic evaluations also remain absent across several conditions for which evidence of MBSR's clinical benefit continues to accumulate, including posttraumatic stress disorder, sleep disorders, clinician burnout, substance use disorders, migraine, arthritis, and other chronic health conditions.
This systematic review found that MBSR was associated with favorable economic outcomes, particularly in chronic pain populations.

Across healthcare settings, analytic perspectives, and study designs, MBSR was associated with similar or improved outcomes at comparable or lower costs, with savings driven by reductions in healthcare utilization and, where examined, improvements in worker productivity.

Quality assessments were conducted independently by two reviewers (RLA and RG).
Following RG's departure from the study team, a third reviewer (NAL) independently reviewed the assessments and completed additional evaluations as needed.
Any discrepancies were discussed and resolved by consensus between RLA and NAL.

The Quality of Health Economic Studies (QHES) instrument is a 16-item tool that evaluates the methodological quality of economic analyses, including study design, data sources, analytic methods, handling of uncertainty, and transparency of reporting.
Studies were assigned an overall QHES quality score on a standardized 0-100 scale, with higher scores indicating greater methodological rigor.

The QHES criteria evaluate whether studies clearly define objectives and analytic perspective, use high-quality data sources, and apply appropriate methods for measuring and valuing costs and outcomes.

It also assesses critical analytic components, including incremental analysis, handling of uncertainty (e.g., statistical and sensitivity analyses), appropriate time horizons and discounting, and the validity and reliability of outcome measures.

In addition, the QHES criteria emphasize transparency in reporting, requiring clear description of model structure, assumptions, data abstraction methods, and potential sources of bias, as well as justification of conclusions and disclosure of funding sources.

Evidence level was classified using a modified Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine hierarchy consistent with JAMA Health Forum recommendations: Level 1, Properly powered and conducted randomized clinical trial; systematic review with meta-analysis; Level 2, Well-designed controlled trial without randomization; prospective comparative cohort trial; Level 3, Case-control studies; retrospective cohort study; Level 4, Case series with or without intervention; cross-sectional study; Level 5, Opinion of respected authorities; case reports.
Quality rating did not include economic outcome-related statistical power into evidence level assignments because studies are typically powered for clinical outcomes rather than economic outcomes.
CHEERS 2022 is a 28-item checklist developed by the International Society for Pharmacoeconomics and Outcomes Research to promote transparency and consistency in economic evaluation reporting.
Adherence to CHEERS 2022 reporting standards was summarized descriptively as the proportion of applicable items reported per study.
Consistent with guidance for reporting checklists, aggregate CHEERS scores were not interpreted as measures of methodological quality.
Studies were eligible if they evaluated standard MBSR delivered according to the intervention manual (e.g., in a guided group-based format, including in-person or synchronous online delivery).

Minor protocol modifications consistent with pragmatic clinical implementation were permitted (acceptable modifications include reducing or removing the all-day retreat, shortening the weekly sessions by up to 30% from the standard 2.5 hours, shortening the number of weekly sessions up to 25% from the standard 8 weekly sessions).
Studies combining MBSR with usual clinical care or closely related mindfulness-based interventions were eligible, provided that MBSR remained a core intervention component.

text.text: Two RCT-based CUAs, 1,2 two model-based CUAs, 3, 4 and two partial economic evaluations 5, 6 evaluated MBSR among chronic low back pain, chronic neck/back pain, fibromyalgia, bodily distress syndrome, and medically unexplained symptom populations.

text.text: Sample sizes ranged from 93 to 342 participants, and all but one study incorporated time horizons of at least one year.

Although medically unexplained symptoms and bodily distress syndrome are not defined solely by pain, they commonly involve persistent pain and other somatic symptoms and were therefore included within the chronic pain and related persistent somatic symptom category.

Across these studies, MBSR was consistently associated with economically favorable findings when compared with treatment as usual and economically comparable findings when compared with active behavioral comparators.

Both model-based studies projected greater economic value among individuals with high-impact chronic pain 3, 4 , and one additionally projected greater value among older adults. 4 Partial economic evaluations additionally suggested reductions in healthcare utilization, outpatient utilization, and disability-related costs among patients with bodily distress syndrome and medically unexplained symptoms.

text.text: Incremental QALY gain was 0.034 (95% CI: 0.008 to 0.060), with approximately 90% probability of cost-effectiveness at a willingness-to-pay threshold of $50,000/QALY.

Herman (2020) used a Markov model to extend these findings; 3 the model facilitates comparisons across interventions not directly compared in trials, using consistent outcome measures after balancing the baseline mix of patients.
Model results predicted that the costeffectiveness of MBSR is similar to CBT for a typical patient mix, but MBSR is twice as effective for those with high-impact chronic pain.
Outcomes also differed by pain impact level, emphasizing the need to measure CLBP subgroups.

Leininger (2023; thesis), 4 a similar modeling study using different comparators and subgroups, predicted MBSR to be dominant over the base case of home exercise and advice, and the value of MBSR treatment was increased for hypothetical populations of high-impact pain and advanced age (80-year-old population).

Authors note that in this model, the cost-effectiveness of MBSR is comparable to therapies that are often covered by insurance for chronic pain conditions: massage, CBT, and spinal manipulation therapy.

text.text: Delivery costs ranged from £2,234 to £4,128 per group (approximately $3,515 -$6,495 in 2025 USD) and were highly sensitive to actual session attendance.

Although groups were intended to include approximately seven participants, average attendance ranged from only 1.75 to 2.75 participants per session, resulting in relatively high per-participant delivery costs of £1,211 to £1,538 ($1905-$2419).
The authors concluded that alternative delivery formats, such as remote or online programs, may improve participation and reduce per-participant costs.
Seven studies incorporated formal uncertainty analyses to address the substantial variability and skew commonly observed in healthcare expenditure data (QHES item #5).
Methods included nonparametric bootstrap resampling, probabilistic sensitivity analyses, scenario analyses, threshold analyses, and cost-effectiveness acceptability curves.
Despite wide confidence intervals for incremental cost estimates that crossed zero, economic findings remained directionally favorable across many sensitivity analyses and modeled assumptions.

Herman et al. (2017) reported approximately 90% probability of costeffectiveness at a willingness-to-pay threshold of $50,000/QALY despite broad incremental cost confidence intervals. 1 Similarly, Meng et al. (2025) reported an 83.6% probability of costeffectiveness at the same willingness-to-pay threshold. 11  Leininger (2023) additionally demonstrated economically favorable findings across multiple sensitivity and scenario analyses, with larger and more statistically robust cost differences observed from a governmental perspective and per-protocol analyses, 2 and stronger cost-effectiveness estimates projected among patients with high-impact chronic pain and older adults. 3, 4 Saha et al. (2020) conducted uncertainty analyses using nonparametric bootstrapping with 5,000 replications, cost-effectiveness planes, and cost-effectiveness acceptability curves. 8 Although QALY differences between groups were small and statistically nonsignificant (incremental QALY gain: -0.003, 95% CI [-0.008 to 0.001]), incremental costs consistently favored mindfulness group therapy from both healthcare and societal perspectives.

text.text: However, these differences were no longer observed when utilization and costs were assessed over a 2-year follow-up period, suggesting that the short-term reductions in healthcare use were not maintained over time.
The authors speculated that ongoing meditation practice and continued support may be necessary to sustain longer-term benefits.

For breast cancer survivors, Lengacher et al. projected outcomes over a 20-year survival horizon, showing MBSR value accruing over time. 10 They used a 3% annual discount rate on QALY gains and no additional costs, yielding a discounted provider cost per QALY gained of $457 (≈$595 in 2025 USD) and a discounted patient opportunity cost per QALY gained of $407 (≈$530 in 2025 USD), evaluating the direct and opportunity costs of MBSR to providers and patients per QALY gained.

text.text: In this analysis, patient opportunity costs were calculated from participant-reported annual income, which was converted to an hourly wage and multiplied by the total time spent participating in the six-week MBSR(BC) program, including class attendance and travel to and from the intervention site.

Additional participant-incurred costs associated with program participation, including transportation (e.g., gas or bus fare), childcare, meals, and lodging for those traveling longer distances, were also included in the opportunity cost estimate.
